text: Amazon.com, Inc. was incorporated in 1994 in the state of Washington and reincorporated in 1996 in the state of Delaware. The company’s principal corporate offices are located in Seattle, Washington, and it completed its initial public offering in May 1997. Its common stock is listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “AMZN.” As used in this document, “Amazon.com,” “we,” “our,” and similar terms include Amazon.com, Inc. and its subsidiaries, unless the context indicates otherwise. The company operates with a focus on being Earth’s most customer-centric company, guided by four principles: customer obsession rather than competitor focus, passion for invention, commitment to operational excellence, and long-term thinking. It serves five primary customer sets: consumers, sellers, developers, enterprises, and content creators, and provides advertising services through programs such as sponsored ads, display, and video advertising. The company’s operations are organized into three segments: North America, International, and Amazon Web Services (“AWS”), which reflect how the company evaluates performance and manages operations. Segment net sales information is detailed in Item 8 of Part II, “Financial Statements and Supplementary Data — Note 10 — Segment Information.” The financial results of Whole Foods Market, Inc. (“Whole Foods Market”) have been included in the consolidated financial statements from the date of acquisition on August 28, 2017. For consumers, Amazon offers products through its online and physical stores, emphasizing selection, price, and convenience, with customers accessing offerings via websites, mobile apps, Alexa, devices, streaming, and in-store visits. The company manufactures and sells electronic devices such as Kindle, Fire tablet, Fire TV, Echo, Ring, and other devices, and develops and produces media content. It aims to provide customers with low prices, fast and free delivery, easy-to-use functionality, and timely customer service. Amazon Prime, a membership program, includes unlimited free shipping on over 100 million items, access to unlimited streaming of tens of thousands of movies and TV episodes—including Amazon Original content—and other benefits. Customer orders are fulfilled through North America and International fulfillment and delivery networks, co-sourced and outsourced arrangements in certain countries, digital delivery, and physical stores. The company operates global customer service centers, supplemented by co-sourced arrangements. Sellers are supported through programs that enable them to grow their businesses, sell products in Amazon’s stores, and fulfill orders via Amazon, with Amazon not acting as the seller of record. The company earns revenue from fixed fees, a percentage of sales, per-unit activity fees, interest, or a combination of these.

Amazon offers its customers a wide range of products and services through various channels, including mobile apps, Alexa devices, streaming platforms, and physical store visits. The company manufactures and sells electronic devices such as Kindle, Fire tablet, Fire TV, Echo, Ring, and other products, and also develops and produces media content. Amazon aims to provide customers with low prices, fast and free delivery, easy-to-use functionality, and timely customer service. A key offering is Amazon Prime, a membership program that provides unlimited free shipping on over 100 million items, access to unlimited streaming of tens of thousands of movies and TV episodes—including Amazon Original content—and other benefits. Customer orders are fulfilled through North America and International fulfillment and delivery networks, co-sourced and outsourced arrangements in certain countries, digital delivery, and physical stores. Global customer service centers are operated, supplemented by co-sourced arrangements. Amazon provides programs for sellers to grow their businesses, sell products in its stores, and fulfill orders through the platform, earning fixed fees, a percentage of sales, per-unit activity fees, interest, or a combination thereof, without being the seller of record. Through its AWS segment, Amazon serves developers and enterprises of all sizes—including start-ups, government agencies, and academic institutions—by offering a broad range of global compute, storage, database, and other service offerings. The company supports content creators such as authors, independent publishers, musicians, filmmakers, skill and app developers via Kindle Direct Publishing, which allows them to choose royalty options and publish books in the Kindle Store, alongside Amazon Publishing. Amazon competes in a rapidly evolving and intensely competitive global marketplace with a broad array of competitors from various industries, including physical and e-commerce retailers, publishers, media distributors, web search engines, comparison shopping sites, social networks, online platforms, e-commerce service providers, fulfillment and logistics companies, IT service providers, consumer electronics manufacturers, and online grocery retailers. Key competitive factors in its retail businesses are selection, price, and convenience, especially fast and reliable fulfillment, while for seller and enterprise services, quality, speed, and reliability of services and tools, as well as customers’ ability and willingness to change business practices, are important. Some competitors have greater resources, longer histories, more customers, stronger brand recognition, and better control over critical inputs, enabling them to secure better supplier terms, adopt aggressive pricing, impose restrictive distribution agreements, redirect consumers, lock in customers, and invest more in technology, infrastructure, fulfillment, and marketing. The Internet enables easier market entry and comparison shopping, allowing smaller or lesser-known businesses to compete. Each of Amazon’s businesses faces rapid change, emerging business models, and new, well-funded competitors, and some companies may form business combinations or alliances to strengthen their positions. Amazon considers its trademarks, service marks, copyrights, patents, domain names, trade dress, trade secrets, and proprietary technologies critical to its success and protects them through legal frameworks, confidentiality agreements, and licensing arrangements. The company has registered or applied for registration of numerous U.S. and international trademarks, service marks, domain names, and copyrights and has filed U.S. and international patent applications for certain proprietary technologies. Amazon may license its proprietary rights to third parties in the past and expects to do so in the future. The business experiences seasonality, with historically higher sales volume in the fourth quarter, which ends December 31. In 2017, 2018, and 2019, Amazon recognized 34%, 31%, and 31% of its annual revenue during the fourth quarter, respectively, with the 2017 results including revenue from Whole Foods Market, acquired on August 28, 2017. As of December 31, 2019, Amazon employed approximately 798,000 full-time and part-time employees, with employment levels fluctuating due to seasonal factors. The company also uses independent contractors and temporary personnel to supplement its workforce. Works councils, statutory employee representation obligations, and union agreements exist in certain countries outside the United States and at some studio operations in the U.S. Amazon considers its employee relations to be good, though competition for qualified personnel—particularly software engineers, computer scientists, and other technical staff—has been historically intense. Investor information is available on Amazon’s investor relations website, amazon.com/ir, where free, timely access is provided to SEC filings, corporate governance materials, including the Code of Business Conduct and Ethics, and select press releases. The company faces intense competition across geographies and industries, including physical, e-commerce, and omnichannel retail, e-commerce services, web and infrastructure computing services, electronic devices, digital content, advertising, grocery, and transportation and logistics. Competitors have greater resources, longer histories, more customers, and stronger brand recognition, especially in new products, services, and geographic regions, and may secure better vendor terms, adopt aggressive pricing, or invest more in technology, infrastructure, fulfillment, and marketing. New business models, alliances, and market expansions by competitors further intensify competition, while emerging technologies such as search, web services, digital content, and electronic devices increase competitive pressure. The Internet enables easier market entry and comparison shopping, allowing smaller or lesser-known businesses to compete effectively. As a result, the company’s product and service offerings may fail, it may lose or fail to gain business, and it may need to increase spending or lower prices, all of which could materially reduce sales and profits. The company’s rapid global expansion places significant strain on management, operations, financial resources, systems, technical performance, and internal financial controls. Failure to manage growth effectively could harm its reputation, limit growth, and negatively affect operating results. Expansion into new products, services, technologies, and geographic regions introduces risks due to limited or no prior experience, potential customer resistance, technology challenges, service disruptions, or quality issues, and the possibility that profitability will not meet expectations or that investments will not be recouped. The company experiences significant fluctuations in operating results and growth rates due to difficulties in forecasting growth, fixed expenses, and slow spending adjustments when sales fall short of estimates. Revenue and operating profit growth depend on demand for its products and services or those of its sellers, which are influenced by global economic and business conditions. A decline in demand, due to changing customer preferences or economic weakness, could reduce revenue or growth. Sales and operating results also fluctuate due to customer retention, network expansion, product pricing, inventory management, fulfillment, competitive product launches, changes in Internet and e-commerce adoption, system upgrade timing and costs, geographic and product line expansion success, financing terms, legal outcomes, product mix variations, vendor returns, delivery benefits, brand reputation, technology investments, rising fuel and commodity prices, network fee collection, collections of receivables, cybersecurity threats like spyware, viruses, phishing, denial of service attacks, data theft, and outages, and disruptions from natural or man-made disasters, geopolitical events, labor or trade disputes. International operations are significant to revenue and profit and are expected to grow further, but the company has limited experience in certain international segments and may not achieve first-mover advantages. Establishing and maintaining international operations is costly, and profitability may not be sustained. International operations face risks such as local economic and political conditions, government regulation, trade protection measures, nationalization, restrictions on sales or distribution, legal uncertainties regarding liability and intellectual property, business licensing requirements, limitations on repatriating funds or investing abroad, foreign exchange restrictions, limited fulfillment and technology infrastructure, and shorter payable and longer receivable cycles.

Amazon has limited operating experience in international markets and may not gain first-to-market advantages or achieve success. Establishing, developing, and maintaining international operations and stores, as well as promoting the brand globally, is costly, and international operations may not become profitable on a sustained basis. International sales and operations face various risks, including local economic and political conditions, government regulation (such as product and competition rules), restrictive actions like trade protection measures, export duties, quotas, tariffs, nationalization, and foreign ownership restrictions; limitations on product or service sales and uncertainty about liability due to less Internet-friendly legal systems, lack of legal precedent, and differing rules on media distribution and intellectual property enforcement; business licensing or certification needs for imports, exports, web services, and electronic devices; restrictions on repatriating funds and foreign currency exchange; limited fulfillment and technology infrastructure; shorter payable and longer receivable cycles that negatively impact cash flow; consumer and data protection, privacy, network security, encryption, payment, advertising, and pricing regulations; lower Internet usage; reduced consumer spending and growth opportunities compared to the U.S.; lower credit card usage and higher payment risk; difficulties in staffing, developing, and managing foreign operations due to distance, language, and cultural differences; different employee-employer relationships, including works councils and labor unions; compliance with the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other laws prohibiting corrupt payments; trade, foreign investment, loan, and tax regulations in the U.S. and other jurisdictions; and geopolitical events such as war and terrorism. As international physical, e-commerce, and omnichannel retail and other services grow, competition intensifies, with local companies having a significant advantage due to their deeper understanding of local customers and established brand presence. The inability to hire, train, retain, and manage sufficient personnel may hinder international growth. The People’s Republic of China (PRC) and India regulate Amazon and its affiliates’ operations through laws and licensing requirements that may restrict (i) foreign investment in Internet, IT infrastructure, data centers, retail, delivery, and other sectors, (ii) Internet content, and (iii) the sale of media and other products and services. For example, in China, Amazon provides certain technology services through contractual arrangements with third parties that hold PRC licenses; in India, the government restricts foreign ownership of Indian companies involved in online multi-brand retail trading. For www.amazon.in, Amazon provides marketing tools and logistics services to third-party sellers and holds indirect minority interests in entities that are third-party sellers on the marketplace. Although these structures are believed to comply with current laws, they carry unique risks, and the PRC and India may introduce new regulatory or licensing changes that could affect them. There are significant uncertainties in interpreting PRC and Indian laws, and the governments might take a position contrary to Amazon’s. Additionally, Amazon’s Chinese and Indian operations could cease if Amazon or its affiliates cannot access sufficient funding or, in China, enforce existing contracts. Violations of existing or future PRC, Indian, or other laws or changes in their interpretation could lead to fines, license revocation, operational restructuring, or complete shutdown. Amazon also faces risks related to optimizing and operating its fulfillment network and data centers; failure to accurately predict customer demand or effectively manage these networks can result in excess or insufficient capacity, increased costs, and impairment charges, which could materially harm the business. As Amazon expands fulfillment and data center capabilities or enters new businesses with different needs, the networks become more complex and harder to operate, and there is no guarantee of effective operation. Poor inventory optimization increases net shipping costs through long-zone or partial shipments. Amazon and its co-sourcers may lack sufficient staffing for fulfillment and customer service centers. Under some commercial agreements, Amazon maintains inventory for other companies, increasing inventory tracking complexity and the risk of failure to secure storage or optimize operations if demand forecasts are inaccurate. Amazon relies on a limited number of shipping companies to deliver inventory and completed orders, and difficulties in negotiating terms or performance issues with these companies or disruptions in Amazon’s own transportation systems could harm operating results and customer experience. Natural or man-made disasters, extreme weather, geopolitical events, security issues, labor or trade disputes, and similar events could also negatively affect inbound inventory receipt and order shipping. The retail business is seasonal, with a disproportionate share of sales occurring in the fourth quarter. Failure to stock or restock popular products adequately could reduce revenue and future growth. Overstocking may require significant markdowns or write-offs and commitment costs, reducing profitability. Net shipping costs rise due to complimentary upgrades, split-shipments, and long-zone shipments during the holiday season. High demand could cause system interruptions, making websites unavailable or hindering order fulfillment, reducing product offerings and attractiveness. Staffing shortages in fulfillment and customer service centers, as well as difficulties from fulfillment and co-sourcer partners, may occur during peak periods, and fulfillment and inventory risks are amplified during high demand. Our business faces significant risks related to commercial relationships, including commitments that may limit the volume of services we can provide. We may struggle to implement, maintain, and develop components of these agreements—such as web services, fulfillment, customer service, inventory management, tax collection, payment processing, hardware, content, and third-party software—and may need to rely on third parties to perform services. Compensation under certain agreements depends on the volume of the other company’s sales; if their offerings fail, we may receive lower-than-expected payments or the agreement may be terminated. We may also be unable to secure new or alternative commercial relationships or strategic alliances on favorable terms, and we could face claims from businesses we serve if we fail to deliver on these services. As agreements expire, we may not be able to renew or replace them on comparable terms or at all, and we might enter into amendments on less favorable terms or encounter parties who fail to meet their contractual obligations, which could harm our operating results. Our e-commerce services, commercial agreements, and strategic alliances introduce risks such as disruption of ongoing operations, impairment of existing relationships, variability in revenue from entering, amending, or terminating agreements, and difficulties in integration. Acquisitions and investments also pose risks, including disruption of business operations, challenges in retaining key personnel, additional operating losses and expenses, potential impairment of tangible and intangible assets and goodwill, and difficulties in integrating operations, technology, and systems—leading to unanticipated costs and integration challenges. Integration may also strain accounting, financial reporting, management, information security, human resources, and administrative systems, and we may incur losses due to declines in investment value or the incorporation of an investee’s financial performance into our results. For investments where financial performance is included in our results, we depend on the investee’s accounting and financial controls. Acquired companies may require implementation of public company controls, and we face risks specific to the acquired businesses, including unknown liabilities and challenges in integrating operations across different cultures, languages, and jurisdictions due to foreign transactions. Future acquisitions or mergers could require us to issue additional equity, spend cash, incur debt, or face amortization expenses, any of which could reduce profitability or be unavailable on favorable terms. Valuations of acquisitions and investments may change rapidly, and we could determine that such valuations have declined in fair value, negatively impacting financial results. Our international operations are exposed to foreign exchange rate fluctuations, which can materially affect operating results and intercompany balance remeasurement, with increased exposure due to expansion. We hold cash equivalents and marketable securities in foreign currencies such as British Pounds, Euros, and Japanese Yen; when the U.S. Dollar strengthens, these balances translate to lower values, and vice versa. We rely heavily on senior management, particularly Jeffrey P. Bezos, our President, CEO, and Chairman, and do not have key person life insurance policies. Competition for skilled personnel, especially in technology fields like software engineering and computer science, is intense, and the loss of any executive or key employee, or our inability to hire, train, retain, or manage qualified staff, could harm our business. We are also vulnerable to data loss, theft, misuse, or security breaches due to the large volume of sensitive, confidential, and proprietary data we process, store, and transmit. Although we use third-party systems for encryption, authentication, email, content delivery, and back-office functions and have implemented protective measures, these cannot guarantee absolute security and may fail or be circumvented. Past breaches have not had a material adverse effect, but future incidents could lead to loss, disclosure, or misuse of data, litigation, regulatory action under privacy or data protection laws, customer or seller attrition, and reputational harm. We experience occasional system interruptions or delays that affect website availability, order processing, and service delivery, reducing net sales and product attractiveness. Upgrades to systems and infrastructure may not fully prevent such disruptions. Our systems are vulnerable to natural or man-made disasters, extreme weather, geopolitical events, cyberattacks, break-ins, and other disruptions, which could cause data loss, service interruptions, and liability. Our systems lack full redundancy, disaster recovery planning may be insufficient, and insurance may not cover all losses, potentially damaging our reputation and incurring high remediation costs. We face significant inventory risks due to seasonality, new product launches, rapid product cycle changes, pricing shifts, defective goods, changing consumer demand, shifting tastes, spoilage, and other factors. While we attempt to forecast demand and avoid over- or understocking, demand can change between order placement and sale. Launching new products may involve difficulties in establishing vendor relationships, selecting components, and forecasting demand. Certain inventory purchases require long lead times, prepayment, and are non-returnable. We maintain broad and high inventory levels for products like consumer electronics, and at times we cannot sell sufficient quantities or meet demand during peak seasons. Any of these inventory risks could negatively impact operating results. Additionally, we face risks related to protecting our intellectual property and being accused of infringing third-party intellectual property

Defective merchandise, shifts in consumer demand and spending patterns, changes in consumer preferences regarding our products, spoilage, and other factors pose inventory risks. We strive to accurately forecast these trends to avoid overstocking or understocking, but demand can change significantly between the time inventory or components are ordered and the date of sale. When launching a new product, establishing vendor relationships, selecting appropriate components, and forecasting demand can be challenging. Acquiring certain inventory or components often requires long lead times, prepayment, and may not be returnable. We maintain a broad selection and high inventory levels for products like consumer electronics, and at times, we are unable to sell sufficient quantities or meet demand during key selling seasons. Any of these inventory risks could negatively impact our operating results. We consider our trademarks, service marks, copyrights, patents, trade dress, trade secrets, and proprietary technology essential to our success and rely on legal protections and confidentiality or license agreements to safeguard these rights. However, effective intellectual property protection is not available in all countries where our products and services are offered, and we may not secure appropriate domain names globally. Regulations on domain names may not protect our trademarks or proprietary rights, and third parties may acquire domain names similar to or infringing on our rights, diminishing their value. We may not always detect unauthorized use of our intellectual property, and third-party licensing actions could reduce the value of our rights or reputation. Protecting our intellectual property requires substantial financial and managerial resources, and our protective measures may not fully prevent infringement or misappropriation. We cannot be certain that others will not independently develop or acquire equivalent or superior technologies. We have faced and expect to continue facing claims alleging infringement of third parties’ intellectual property rights, which, even if not meritorious, can result in significant financial and managerial costs, injunctions, or damages, including to satisfy indemnification obligations or to obtain licenses. Such licenses may not be available on acceptable terms or at all. These risks are heightened by the growing number of third parties who specialize in filing such claims. Our digital content relies on digital rights management technology to control access; breaches or malfunctions could lead to claims and cause content providers to refuse to include their content. Our business model is rapidly evolving, and our common stock price experiences significant volatility due to factors such as changes in interest rates, trends in the Internet and our industry segments, quarterly operating results, general stock market fluctuations, especially in Internet-related companies, changes in financial estimates or spending decisions, analyst recommendations, changes in capital structure, shifts in the valuation of other e-commerce or technology companies, and trading activity by major investors or analyst reports. This volatility could harm our business, financing capabilities, and force us to increase employee cash compensation or grant larger stock awards, which could negatively affect operating results or reduce existing stockholder ownership. We are subject to a wide range of general and industry-specific regulations, including those related to taxation, privacy, data protection, pricing, content, copyrights, distribution, transportation, mobile communications, electronic device certification, electronic waste, energy consumption, environmental standards, electronic contracts, competition, consumer protection, employment, trade policies, web services, online payments, registration, licensing, information reporting, unencumbered access to our services, website design and operation, health and safety, product quality and labeling, unmanned aircraft systems, and more. The application of existing laws to areas like property ownership, libel, data protection, and privacy in digital and e-commerce contexts is unclear. Many jurisdictions regulate our operations, and the scope and nature of these regulations are expanding as our business grows. We regularly face formal and informal reviews and investigations by government authorities, such as the European Commission’s investigation into potential violations of EU competition rules by our marketplace seller operations. Unfavorable regulations, legal decisions, or enforcement actions could lead to substantial costs, civil or criminal penalties, reduced demand for our products or services, increased operating costs, required changes to business practices, reputational damage, or hindered growth. We are also regularly subject to actual or threatened claims, litigation, investigations, and proceedings involving intellectual property, taxes, labor, competition, privacy, consumer protection, commercial disputes, and third-party offerings. The number and complexity of these proceedings have increased with our global expansion and operational scale. These proceedings can disrupt operations, divert management attention, generate negative publicity, and incur legal costs, with outcomes that are inherently uncertain. Estimating potential losses involves judgment and may not capture all uncertainties, and we could be exposed to losses exceeding recorded amounts, which might be material. Changes in assumptions or estimates could materially affect our financial position, results of operations, or cash flows. A resolution of any such proceeding—through settlement or otherwise—could require licenses, sanctions, consent decrees, or substantial future payments, restrict product or service offerings, mandate significant changes to business practices, require development of non-infringing alternatives, damage our reputation, or otherwise materially impact our operations. We are also subject to various taxes and tax collection obligations in the U.S. (federal and state) and numerous foreign

A resolution of one or more legal proceedings, including through settlement, could involve licenses, sanctions, consent decrees, or orders requiring substantial future payments, restricting our ability to offer certain products or services, mandating significant changes to our business practices that are materially adverse to our operations, requiring the development of non-infringing or altered products or technologies, damaging our reputation, or otherwise having a material impact on our operations. We are subject to a wide range of taxes and tax collection obligations in the U.S. (federal and state) and numerous foreign jurisdictions. We may incur additional tax expenses and liabilities due to changes in tax laws, regulations, administrative practices, principles, or interpretations—such as changes to the global tax framework, competition, or accounting rules—driven by economic, political, or other conditions. An increasing number of jurisdictions are considering or have implemented new tax measures, including revenue-based taxes targeting online commerce and remote sales, such as obligations to collect sales, consumption, value-added, or other taxes on online marketplaces and remote sellers, or requirements that may result in liability for third-party obligations. For example, the European Union, certain member states, and other countries have proposed or enacted taxes on online advertising and marketplace service revenues. Additional taxes imposed prospectively or retroactively, or penalties from failing to comply with collection obligations or to provide information about customers, suppliers, or other third parties to government agencies, could adversely affect our results of operations and cash flows. In some cases, we may not receive sufficient notice to implement systems or processes to comply with new reporting or collection obligations by their effective dates. Our tax expense and liabilities are also influenced by changes in business operations, acquisitions, investments, entry into new businesses or geographies, intercompany transactions, the level of foreign earnings, losses in jurisdictions where tax benefits cannot be realized, the application of special tax regimes, foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations, changes in stock price, and changes in deferred tax assets and liabilities and their valuations. Significant judgment is required in estimating tax expenses and liabilities, as many transactions involve uncertain tax outcomes. For instance, the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (the “U.S. Tax Act”) introduced complex computations, significant judgments in interpreting its provisions, substantial estimates, and new information not previously produced or regularly analyzed. The U.S. Treasury Department, the IRS, and other standard-setting bodies will continue to issue guidance on how the U.S. Tax Act is applied, and as such, we may adjust previously recorded amounts, which could materially impact our financial statements in the period of adjustment. We are also subject to tax controversies in various jurisdictions that can lead to tax assessments. Developments in audits, investigations, or other tax disputes can materially affect our operating results or cash flows in the relevant periods, as well as prior and subsequent periods. We regularly assess the likelihood of adverse outcomes to determine if our tax accruals are adequate. Although we believe our tax estimates are reasonable, the final outcomes of audits, investigations, or tax controversies could differ materially from our historical accruals. We have significant suppliers, including content and technology licensors, and in some cases, limited or single-source supply, which are critical to our sourcing, services, manufacturing, and ongoing servicing of merchandise and content. Most of our suppliers do not have long-term agreements guaranteeing availability of merchandise, content, components, or services, specific payment terms, or credit limits. If suppliers decide to cease selling or licensing merchandise, content, components, or services on acceptable terms, or delay delivery—due to supplier bankruptcies from poor economic conditions, natural disasters, or other reasons—we may be unable to quickly or efficiently source alternatives on acceptable terms or at all. Additionally, violations by suppliers or vendors of applicable laws, regulations, contractual terms, intellectual property rights of others, or our Supply Chain Standards, or the use of products or practices deemed unethical, unsafe, or hazardous, could result in claims, reputational damage, limited growth, and negative impacts on our operating results. Our contracts with U.S. and foreign government entities—including state, local, and foreign governments—are subject to various procurement regulations and requirements related to formation, administration, and performance. We face audits and investigations related to these contracts, and any violations could result in civil and criminal penalties, administrative sanctions, including contract termination, refunding or suspending payments, forfeiture of profits, payment of fines, and suspension or debarment from future government business. Some contracts also allow for termination by the government at any time without cause. We are exposed to product liability claims when products we sell or manufacture cause personal injury, illness, death, environmental or property damage, or require product recalls. Third parties using our services to sell products increase our liability exposure, especially if those sellers lack adequate protection. Although we maintain liability insurance, we cannot be certain it will be sufficient to cover actual liabilities or that coverage will remain available on economically reasonable terms or at all. Banks’ costs, subject to fines and higher transaction fees, and the loss of our ability to accept credit and debit card payments from customers, process electronic funds transfers, or facilitate other online payments could adversely affect our business and operating results. We provide regulated services in certain jurisdictions because we enable customers to hold account balances with us and transfer money to third parties, and because we offer services to third parties to facilitate payments on their behalf. These jurisdictions impose requirements for licensing, regulatory inspections, bonding, and capital maintenance, as well as rules regarding the use, handling, and segregation of transferred funds, consumer disclosures, data maintenance or processing, and authentication. We are also subject to or voluntarily comply with various laws and regulations related to payments, money laundering, international money transfers, privacy, information security, and electronic fund transfers. If found in violation of applicable laws or regulations, we could face additional requirements, civil or criminal penalties, or be forced to stop providing certain services. We are also impacted by fraudulent or unlawful activities of sellers. The legal liability of online service providers remains unsettled, and governmental agencies may require changes in how the business is conducted. Under our seller programs, we have policies and processes to prevent sellers from collecting payments when buyers do not receive ordered products or when products differ materially from descriptions, and to stop sellers from offering unlawful, counterfeit, pirated, or stolen goods, selling goods in an unlawful or unethical manner, violating others’ proprietary rights, or otherwise violating our policies. When these policies and processes fail or are circumvented, our business or reputation may be harmed, and we could face civil or criminal liability for sellers’ unlawful activities. Under our A2Z Guarantee, we reimburse buyers for payments up to certain limits in these cases, and as third-party seller sales grow, the cost of this program will increase and could negatively impact our operating results. As of December 31, 2019, we operated the following facilities (in thousands): office space totaling 18,051 and 15,863 square feet in North America and International respectively, physical stores totaling 20,072 and 169 square feet in North America and International respectively, and fulfillment, data centers, and other facilities totaling 187,148 and 76,868 square feet in North America and International respectively, with total leased and owned square footage of 318,171 and 15,615 respectively. This includes 564 North America and 7 International stores as of December 31, 2019. Segment-wise, North America had 199,473 and 1,983 square feet, International had 74,231 and 958 square feet, and AWS had 10,553 and 5,882 square feet, with total segment leased and owned square footage of 284,257 and 8,823 respectively. Segment amounts exclude corporate facilities, and shared facilities are allocated based on usage, primarily relating to technology infrastructure. We own and lease our corporate headquarters in Seattle, Washington and Arlington, Virginia. As a result of adopting new accounting guidance on January 1, 2019, the company recognized lease assets and liabilities for operating leases with terms exceeding twelve months. Prior period amounts were not adjusted and remain reported under the company’s historical accounting policies. This information, along with additional details, is available in Item 8 of Part II, “Financial Statements and Supplementary Data — Note 1 — Description of Business and Accounting Policies.” The company’s primary revenue source is the sale of a wide range of products and services to customers, including merchandise and content purchased for resale, third-party seller items, manufactured electronic devices, and media content. Revenue is recognized as gross sales from inventory and as net share of revenue from third-party seller items. The company focuses on increasing unit sales through expanded product selection and offerings across categories. Additional services include compute, storage, database, fulfillment, advertising, publishing, and digital content subscriptions. The financial focus is on long-term, sustainable growth in free cash flows, driven by increasing operating income and efficient management of working capital and cash capital expenditures, including purchases or leases of property and equipment. Operating income increases through higher product and service sales and cost management, partially offset by investments in long-term strategic initiatives, such as improving the customer experience. To boost sales, the company improves the customer experience by lowering prices, enhancing availability, offering faster delivery and performance, increasing selection, producing original content, expanding product categories and services, improving product information, ease of use, reliability, and earning customer trust. The company aims to reduce variable costs per unit and leverage fixed costs. Variable costs include product and content costs, payment processing, picking, packaging, transportation, customer service, AWS operations, and a portion of marketing. Fixed costs include technology infrastructure, online store and digital service development, and fulfillment and delivery network operations. Variable costs typically rise with sales volume, while fixed costs depend on capacity needs, geographic or category expansion. To reduce per-unit variable costs, the company increases direct sourcing, secures supplier discounts, and reduces process defects. To limit fixed cost growth, it improves process efficiencies and maintains a lean culture. Due to its business model, the company turns inventory quickly and has a cash-generating operating cycle, collecting from consumers before payments to suppliers are due. Inventory turnover and accounts payable days vary over time due to product mix, sales mix, in-stock availability, new geographies, product lines, and third-party fulfillment use. Technology and content spending is expected to increase as the company hires computer scientists, designers, software and hardware engineers, and merchandising staff. Investments in AWS and new product categories support geographic expansion and cross-functional systems. The company believes advances in technology—such as faster and cheaper processing power, wireless connectivity, and artificial intelligence and machine learning—will enhance the Internet experience and expand its use. To leverage these advances, the company invests in innovative software and electronic devices and in AWS, which provides global compute, storage, database, and other services to developers and enterprises. The company seeks to manage shareholder dilution while maintaining flexibility for strategic purposes like financings, acquisitions, and employee compensation alignment. Restricted stock units are used as the primary equity compensation tool to align long-term shareholder and employee interests. Shareholder dilution is measured by including all vested and unvested stock awards, without estimating forfeitures. Total shares outstanding plus outstanding stock awards were 507 million and 512 million as of December 31, 2018 and 2019, respectively. The financial reporting currency is the U.S. Dollar, and foreign exchange rate changes significantly impact reported results and trends. A weaker U.S. Dollar relative to international currencies increases consolidated net sales and operating expenses, while a stronger U.S. Dollar decreases them. The company believes its international business diversification benefits shareholders long-term and finds it useful to evaluate operating results both before and after currency effects. Remeasurement of intercompany balances can lead to significant gains or losses due to foreign exchange rate movements, and currency volatilities may continue to impact reported results and trends. The operating cycle is calculated as the number of days of sales in inventory plus the number of days of sales in accounts receivable, minus accounts payable days. The preparation of financial statements in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles ("GAAP") involves estimates and assumptions that impact the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses, and related disclosures of contingent liabilities. The SEC defines critical accounting policies as those that are most significant to the portrayal of a company’s financial condition and results of operations and require the most difficult and subjective judgments, often due to uncertainty in estimating future events. Based on this, the company has identified key critical accounting policies and judgments, including inventories and income taxes. Inventories are valued using the first-in, first-out method and are recorded at the lower of cost and net realizable value, requiring judgments about future disposition methods—such as sales to customers, returns to vendors, or liquidations—and expected recoverable values. These assumptions are inherently uncertain, and changes could lead to material write-downs; for every 1% increase in inventory valuation allowance as of December 31, 2019, the company would record an additional $230 million in cost of sales. Additionally, supplier commitments for electronic device components and products are based on forecasted customer demand, and reducing these commitments could result in additional costs. Income taxes are assessed in the U.S. (federal and state) and numerous foreign jurisdictions, where tax laws, regulations, and interpretations may change significantly due to economic, political, or other factors, requiring substantial judgment in estimating tax provisions and accruals. Factors affecting effective tax rates include changes in business operations, acquisitions, investments, new business entries, intercompany transactions, foreign earnings levels, losses in jurisdictions where tax benefits cannot be realized, special tax regimes, foreign currency exchange rates, stock price changes, deferred tax asset and liability valuations, and changes in tax laws or regulations, including those related to the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 ("U.S. Tax Act"). The U.S. Tax Act introduced complex computations, significant judgments in interpretation, and new estimates, requiring ongoing analysis and potential adjustments to previously recorded income tax amounts, which could materially impact the provision for income taxes in the period of adjustment. The company is also involved in tax controversies in various jurisdictions, where adverse outcomes could materially affect operating results or cash flows, both in the current and prior or future periods. The company regularly evaluates the likelihood of adverse outcomes to assess the adequacy of tax accruals, though the final outcomes of audits or investigations may differ materially from historical provisions. Liquidity and capital resources are primarily derived from cash flows from operations and cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities, which were valued at $41.3 billion and $55.0 billion as of December 31, 2018 and 2019, respectively. Foreign currency holdings were $13.8 billion and $15.3 billion as of those dates, primarily in Euros, British Pounds, and Japanese Yen. Cash provided by operating activities was $30.7 billion in 2018 and $38.5 billion in 2019, driven by cash received from consumer, seller, developer, enterprise, content creator customers, and advertisers, offset by payments for products and services, employee compensation, payment processing, operating leases, and interest on long-term obligations. The increase in operating cash flow in 2019 was primarily due to higher net income excluding non-cash charges like depreciation, amortization, and stock-based compensation. Operating cash flows are also influenced by working capital fluctuations, including seasonality, inventory management, category expansion, timing of cash receipts and payments, vendor payment terms, and foreign exchange rate changes. Investing activities include capital expenditures, leasehold improvements, vendor incentives, asset sales, acquisitions, investments in other companies and intellectual property, and purchases, sales, and maturities of marketable securities. Cash used in investing activities was $(12.4) billion in 2018 and $(24.3) billion in 2019, primarily due to decisions regarding property and equipment purchases or leases and changes in marketable securities. Cash capital expenditures were $11.3 billion in 2018 and $12.7 billion in 2019.
